guideline_text:
General recommendations for dealing with generative AI in studies and teaching
The use of generative AI (GKI) such as ChatGPT has the potential to comprehensively and sustainably transform academic work and educational processes. It can enable personalized learning, support teaching, and promote research. For this reason, Goethe University generally supports the testing and application of GKI in studies and teaching. However, ethical, legal, and, of course, didactic aspects must be considered when using GKI. Therefore, target group-specific recommendations for action were developed in collaboration with a dedicated, interdisciplinary working group comprised of representatives from various status groups. These recommendations are available to you, building upon this general introduction to GKI. With careful planning and preparation, as well as a clear framework for action, generative AI can be a valuable tool in higher education. 

This guide serves as the central introductory page to the topic of generative AI in higher education. Specific recommendations for students and instructors can be found in two further articles:

– Recommendations for Instructors: Using Generative AI in Teaching
– Recommendations for Students: Using Generative AI in Their Studies

. Answers to frequently asked questions on this topic can be found in the FAQ section at the end of this page.

Are you missing any information? Are there any unanswered questions? Do you have suggestions for additions or further explanations? If so, please contact the Generative AI in Teaching Working Group by email ( ag-gki@studiumdigitale.uni-frankfurt.de ) and we will try to incorporate your perspective into the guide. We look forward to your feedback.

General recommendations and advice
Please note the following basic guidelines for using generative artificial intelligence (GKI) tools and the subsequent instructions: Critical reflection: Always critically reflect on the results of AI, as generative AIs are statistical models that reproduce frequently occurring statements and attitudes from pre-processed training data. For example, if biases are present in the training data (e.g., one-sided or distorted representations), these will also be reproduced in the generated results. Depending on the field and the research question, the results can be very useful and accurate, or they can be incorrect and misleading. Intellectual Property: Please note that generative AIs can create content based on existing data, and therefore intellectual property plays a crucial role. For example, copyrighted material may be present in the AI's training data, which could make the generated content problematic. Data that you provide to an AI for review, for instance, may also be copyrighted. Ensure that the information you input and the results you receive do not infringe on any copyrights. Currently, AI programs themselves cannot be considered authors. Depending on the extent of user input into the generated text, either the user is the author, or the result is in the public domain under copyright law. Personal data: Do not enter any personal or sensitive information when using AI tools. In most cases, the operators of these tools are currently based in the United States, and it is impossible to control what happens to the entered data (Schrems II ruling of the European Court of Justice). Even with the consent of the data subjects, rights such as accessing all collected data or having it deleted cannot be exercised, or can only be exercised to a very limited extent. This is incompatible with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Current status: Many aspects of AI technologies are still under negotiation. Therefore, the opportunities, risks, and legal frameworks are subject to change at any time. We strive to keep the information on this page up to date, but cannot guarantee its accuracy. We welcome corrections and suggestions. What is generative artificial intelligence (GKI)?
The term "generative AI" describes AI systems capable of independently creating novel content on demand. These systems learn from data acquired during their training phase and use this knowledge to generate output, for example, in text form. Besides text generation, other examples of generative AI include image generation, music composition, and the generation of program code for application development.

Language Models (LMs) are a subclass of generative AI. These models learn the probability of word sequences in a given language. Large Language Models (LLMs) are very large language models trained on enormous amounts of text data. This enables them to generate human-like text and allows them to be used for a wide variety of tasks. With proper training, they can handle tasks such as machine translation, question-answering systems, text summarization, and more.

As impressive as the results achievable with LLMs are, they should not be confused with knowledge databases. The texts processed during model training are no longer included verbatim in the final product. Therefore, programs like ChatGPT should not be thought of as search engines that look for relevant passages in text corpora and compile answers by copying and pasting. Instead, they are purely statistical models that reproduce statements and attitudes that frequently occur in their training data. What applications and services are available?
Since the available tools are currently evolving very rapidly, we will attempt to provide an overview of existing tool categories here, which will be revisited throughout this guide.  Literature review	Tools in this category offer a variety of functions to support literature research in higher education. They enable students to efficiently find and organize academic literature and identify relevant articles or authors. With these tools, students can search literature databases, create reading lists, or gain an overview of current research on specific topics. Through integration with reference management programs such as Citavi or Zotero, found articles can also be imported directly into the personal library. An example of a tool in this category is Researchrabbit *.

The university library provides an overview of various tools for literature research.
Text production	Tools in this category actively support students in their academic writing practice. With features such as AI autocomplete, automatic citations, formatting according to different writing styles, and plagiarism checks, they assist in writing academic papers. These tools can accelerate the writing process by helping with formulating complex sentences or finding appropriate references. They enable students to further develop their writing skills and adhere to academic standards. An example of a tool in this category is JenniAI *.
Text comprehension	Tools in this category support students' reading comprehension by allowing them to explore and better understand texts interactively. By highlighting terms, passages, or key information within a text and then using an integrated chatbot, students can obtain explanations, definitions, or additional information. These tools can also answer questions or recommend further resources to deepen their understanding of a particular text. These tools are especially useful when students need to read and analyze complex academic texts. They can help students identify meaningful connections and relationships within a text and deepen their understanding. By interacting with a chatbot, students receive personalized support and can further develop their reading comprehension. An example of such a tool is Explainpaper *.
Plagiarism detection	Tools in this category are specifically designed to detect plagiarism in academic work. They enable instructors and students to check all submitted texts for potential similarities with other sources or previously published works. These tools search extensive databases and use advanced algorithms to identify suspicious matches. They help maintain the integrity of academic work and encourage students to work independently and develop their own ideas. An example of a tool in this category is Turnitin *.
Image generation	Tools in this category utilize deep learning algorithms to generate images from text input or to modify existing images. They enable students to create high-quality visual content using descriptions or instructions. These tools are particularly useful for creating images or diagrams for presentations, posters, websites, or reports. Using such tools can save time and resources in material creation and empower students or instructors who lack strong artistic skills or extensive design knowledge and software to produce visually appealing materials. One example of a tool in this category is DreamStudio *, which uses the StableDiffusion model for image generation.
Presentation creation	Tools in this category enable students and instructors to easily create engaging presentations. They are based on text input and automatically generate slides with relevant content. These tools offer various design templates, animation options, and the ability to insert multimedia elements such as images or videos. They simplify the creation of visually appealing presentations and save time. Students and instructors spend less time designing slides and can focus more on the content of their presentations. These tools make it possible to create professional-looking presentations and present information in an accessible and engaging way. An example of a tool in this category is SlidesAI *. Use of generative AI in studies and teaching
In addition to this general introduction to generative AI (including tool categories and collection), there are two further recommendations specifically for teachers and students.  

Use of AI in teaching (target group: teachers)
Use of AI in studies (target group: students)
Further support services on the topic of AI in teaching at Goethe University include:

“Learning about, with and from AI? – An educational tour” (studiumdigitale)
“Potential uses of AI tools in teaching” (studiumdigitale)
"What do we do with AI and what does AI do to us? Ethical aspects of using AI tools in higher education" (studiumdigitale)
“AI applications such as ChatGPT in teaching and examinations” (IKH) 
“Teaching AI-supported writing” (IKH & Writing Center) 
Online teaching lab “ChatGPT as a challenge and an opportunity. What does AI do to writing?” (Writing Center)
Tips for using AI writing tools in teaching (Writing Center)
Impulse series within the framework of the HessenHub joint project How can we ensure that all students/lecturers have access to a tool?
As long as the university itself does not offer suitable solutions, the decision rests with each individual, meaning access cannot be guaranteed. The university is currently working on appropriate solutions, but this is being delayed due to various factors (lack of data protection, insufficient quality of results, rapid development, high resource consumption, and diverse requirements). As soon as a solution is available, it will be communicated here and through the usual channels. Alternative tasks/materials should always be offered that can be completed without AI tools or ChatGPT. Learners/teachers must not be disadvantaged if they do not wish to create an account. In teaching contexts, group work can allow people without their own access to try out the tools or complete tasks. Currently, several scouting processes are underway to identify tools and determine how they can be rolled out at the university. This includes purchasing licenses, the associated data protection processes, and developing in-house solutions. As soon as a solution is available, it will be communicated here and through our usual channels. Issuing prohibitions can always lead to their violation. It's essential to continually question the learning objective and to what extent tools can support, but not replace, achieving that objective. Transparent use of tools and clear rules within the classroom context foster a trusting, creative, and constructive learning environment. Ultimately, however, it remains the responsibility of the teachers to decide whether and for what purpose AI tools may be used. Proving deception when using generative AI tools is currently extremely difficult, as no reliable detection software is available to date, making AI use difficult to verify. While programs like AI Text Classifier or ChatGPT Zero already exist on the market, they are highly error-prone and would not, on their own, constitute sufficient proof of deception. An act of deception occurs, even if AI tools are cited as aids, if the entire exam or significant parts thereof are generated by AI tools, as this negates the independent work involved. However, there is no uniform percentage threshold, and each case must be decided individually. These exist, and you can find examples under "What applications and services are available?" . However, since these are independent services outside the university, they do not constitute recommendations, and you are responsible for ensuring compliance with all legal regulations (data protection, IT security, copyright, accessibility, etc.) should you choose to use them. Please also refer to the General Recommendations and Guidelines on Generative AI .
